summary: This project is a daily astronaut health detection system. In principle, we require astronauts to spend three minutes every morning taking a test, and our system categorizes the test results into three simple indicators—Normal, Caution, and Critical—allowing astronauts to intuitively understand their physical condition at first glance. Returning to the main page provides a more detailed analytical report, and clicking the top-right corner displays the underlying principles of the report so astronauts understand the substantive issues. Additionally, immediate response protocols for corresponding issues appear automatically below whenever a specific issue lights up. Beyond real-time detection, the most important feature is that our website maintains continuous, traceable records starting from the very first day of the mission, enabling users to review their status from previous days or even go all the way back to Day 1. This helps monitor long-term changes in the astronauts' physical condition and provides NASA with more direct data for research. Furthermore, our design concept aims to synchronize this system with ground control so that if an astronaut experiences an issue, it can be observed directly through the system without the astronaut having to send a message manually.
details:
Please note first that because our entire team is Taiwanese, this passage—including the system we developed—was originally written entirely in Chinese, and we used AI to translate it directly into English. Some word choices may not fully reflect what our team intended to express due to discrepancies in AI translation word selection, so we hope you can understand this.

The function of this project is to monitor astronauts' daily physical indicators using the daily three-minute test we implemented, which consists of four assessments in total. The diagnostic report also integrates radiation rates and the number of days spent in outer space, resulting in six diagnostic reports overall: reaction nerves, cardiovascular flow rate, vision, stress, bone density, and radiation. Daily records are kept to make it easier to analyze physical conditions. When an anomaly is detected, the system immediately provides first-response countermeasures, bridging the communication gap when the ground team cannot offer real-time advice, thereby giving astronauts stronger safety protection. Furthermore, retaining these records helps NASA collect data for research, allowing personnel to review an astronaut's daily physical condition on a day-by-day basis across the six mentioned assessments.

For development tools, we coded using Antigravity, uploaded the code to GitHub, and deployed it to Vercel. Because our two-day working timeframe was limited, many parts of the coding required the assistance of AI agents to boost efficiency. We did not spend excessive effort on the system's visual appearance; instead, we focused heavily on functionality and data logging.

The innovative aspect of this project lies in integrating multiple pre-existing indicators to cross-validate and analyze physical conditions—this integration itself is the innovation. Since we are on Earth, we cannot risk astronauts' lives to test brand-new, unverified assessments or metrics. Therefore, the four physical tests included are all adapted from precursors that NASA has already researched. Similarly, the computational models for radiation and bone loss are applied based on existing NASA data. For us, data accuracy and system practicality are far more important than creativity filled with unknowns, so we channeled our innovation into the cross-validation of the reports rather than the testing functions or the data itself.

At the very top of the testing system, there are indicators measuring carbon dioxide, cabin pressure, and radiation. Because our solution is purely software-based without physical testing hardware, it requires connecting to dedicated sensors to receive real data. The same applies to the radiation indicator in the diagnostic report section. Currently, we have populated those areas with simulated data so you can better see how the system operates in practice. Additionally, the website is not currently connected to a live database; whenever the page is refreshed, today's data resets to zero, while yesterday's data is automatically populated with simulated data. This is because we want every judge to be able to see both what the system looks like after a test is completed and how it reminds astronauts to take the test before it is done—preventing a situation where later judges only see the completed state after earlier judges have finished the test. Leaving the database disconnected was intentional so we can better showcase all states of the system.

projectRefs: Regarding the radiation issue you highlighted, as well as the fact that neutron radiation accounts for approximately 30% of the total radiation dose on the International Space Station, we have integrated this into our radiation detection system.

Regarding the diagrams in the article—including those covering the brain, cardiovascular system, and bone loss—our system has corresponding detection mechanisms for each. Furthermore, understanding the issue of communication delays with Earth, when our system detects an anomaly, it will immediately provide the astronauts with corresponding countermeasures.
